title: The desert
hookLine: a monk in an Egyptian cell keeps checking the window to see if the sun has moved

cards: Late morning in a small stone cell in the Egyptian desert. A monk is supposed to be praying and reading. Instead he gets up and looks out the door to see whether the sun has moved.
It hasn't, much. He sits back down. A minute later he's up again, checking whether anyone is coming to visit.

He starts to think the other monks don't care about him, that he'd be holier somewhere else, anywhere else. A monk named Evagrius wrote this scene down, almost like a field guide entry, and gave the restless thing a name.
He wasn't writing to shame the monk. He was mapping the terrain.

teach.h: MONKS AND NUNS IN THE DESERT.
teach.b: The desert, here, means the Christian monks and nuns who went out into the deserts of Egypt and nearby lands to pray, later called the desert fathers and mothers.
Evagrius of Pontus lived among them and wrote short, sharp sayings on the inner life. First, thoughts.

Evagrius uses the Greek word logismoi, thoughts, for the patterns that pull a person away from prayer. In his work called the Praktikos he names eight: gluttony, lust, greed, sadness, anger, acedia, vainglory and pride.
Second, acedia, the one in the hook.
He calls it the noonday demon, the restlessness that makes the day seem endless and every other place look better. Third, watching.
Evagrius advises observing the thoughts closely: when they come, how strong they are, which one follows which. Like a doctor, he studies the pattern rather than just suffering it.
He understood these thoughts as the work of demons, and writes that way. Some readers outside his faith still take up the method: see it clearly, and name it. Fourth, answering.
In another book he gathers short lines of scripture to say back to each thought when it arrives.

teach.h: WATCH IT. NAME IT. ANSWER IT.
teach.b: Name it, then answer it. Some historians trace the later Western list of deadly sins back, through the monk John Cassian, to this desert list. That's a long road from a stone cell and a monk checking the sun.

how: In Orthodox and Catholic monastic life, Evagrius and the desert fathers and mothers are read for guidance on prayer, and some Christians practice noticing and naming troubling thoughts as part of their prayer.

p: the thoughts that pull from prayer

s: Evagrius wrote about the thoughts to shame the monks who had them
he observed them like a doctor, mapping when they came and which followed which.
acedia is a restlessness that makes the day seem endless
the noonday demon: checking the sun, wishing to be anywhere else.
in the Praktikos he names eight, from gluttony to pride.

games.q: you're a monk in the desert cell and the restless thought arrives again. going by Evagrius, what's the first move?
o: leave the cell and find better company.
watch it closely and name it.
games.why: Evagrius advises watching the thoughts closely and naming them, and then answering them with short lines of scripture.

practice: Wait for whatever shows up; it will. When a thought pulls at you, give it a plain one-word name, the way a field guide would: worry, wanting, irritation, restlessness, planning.
Don't argue with it or follow it; just name it and come back to the breath, and if the same one keeps coming, that's useful information, not a failure.

wordCard.voice: The desert. The early Christian monks and nuns of Egypt and beyond, among them Evagrius, who mapped the thoughts that trouble prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: thoughts, Evagrius's word for what troubles prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: name the thought. Even the noonday demon has a name. See you tomorrow.
